title: Neurons, Action Potentials, and Synaptic Transmission
description: Explore the structural anatomy of the neuron, electrochemical signaling, and the all-or-none law.

slides.title: Anatomy of the Neuron 🧬
slides.content:
# The Building Block of the Nervous System

The human brain contains approximately **86 billion neurons**. Each neuron consists of specialized anatomical structures:

* **Dendrites**: Branching extensions that receive chemical messages from neighboring cells.
* **Soma (Cell Body)**: Contains the cell nucleus and maintains metabolic life support.
* **Axon**: Long, slender fiber that conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body toward terminal buttons.
* **Myelin Sheath**: Fatty insulating layer formed by glial cells (Schwann cells / oligodendrocytes) that drastically accelerates impulse conduction.
* **Nodes of Ranvier**: Periodic gaps in the myelin sheath where action potentials regenerate via **saltatory conduction**.
* **Terminal Buttons**: Knobs at the axon tips that house synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters.

quizData.question: Which component of a neuron is primarily responsible for receiving incoming chemical signals from other neurons?
quizData.explanation: Dendrites are branching structures specialized to receive incoming neurotransmitter messages from adjacent neurons.

slides.title: The Action Potential ⚡
slides.content:
## Electrochemical Firing of a Neuron

Communication within a neuron is **electrical**, governed by ion movements across the semi-permeable cell membrane.

| Phase | Membrane Potential | Primary Ion Movement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Resting State** | Approximately -70 mV | Sodium ($Na^+$) outside, Potassium ($K^+$) inside |
| **Depolarization** | Reaches threshold (-55 mV) | Voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels snap open, $Na^+$ rushes in |
| **Peak Action Potential**| Surges to +30 to +40 mV | $Na^+$ channels close; $K^+$ channels open |
| **Repolarization** | Plummets back downward | $K^+$ ions rapidly exit the cell |
| **Refractory Period** | Hyperpolarized below -70 mV | Sodium-Potassium pumps restore baseline ion balance |

### The All-or-None Principle
A neuron either fires completely or does not fire at all. A stronger stimulus causes the neuron to fire **more frequently**, never with a 'stronger' electrical voltage.

slides.title: Common Misconceptions ⚠️
slides.content:
### Neural Speed is Not the Speed of Light!

Unlike electricity flowing through a copper wire at near light speed, neural action potentials travel between **1 and 120 meters per second** because they rely on chemical ion exchange across physical membranes.

Damage to the myelin sheath impairs this transmission, as seen in **Multiple Sclerosis (MS)**, leading to motor weakness, loss of coordination, and visual impairments.

quizData.question: According to the All-or-None Law, how does the nervous system encode a very intense stimulus (such as a scalding hot pan) compared to a mild warmth?

options.text: By producing action potentials with 10x higher voltage
By increasing the frequency and total number of neurons firing
By slowing down the speed of the action potential

quizData.explanation: Because individual action potentials cannot vary in size, stimulus intensity is coded via firing rate (frequency) and recruitment of multiple neurons.

slides.title: Memory Pathway Hook 💡
slides.content:
## Remember DSAT for Neural Impulse Flow

Follow the electrical journey:
* **D**endrite (Receives signal)
* **S**oma (Integrates threshold)
* **A**xon (Propagates electrical wave)
* **T**erminal Button (Releases chemical neurotransmitters)
